title: kernel-granularity-locality-heatmap-labnotes
content:
Purpose and scope:
This is a working lab notebook documenting an investigation into how attention kernel granularity (tile/block sizes, warp assignment, fused-op grouping) interacts with memory locality (L2, L1, shared memory) across FlashAttention, paged attention, and the fused-ops codepath. Goal: identify reproducible regimes where locality patterns drive tail latency or utilization collapse and propose a low-risk kernel-selection heuristic to avoid the worst cases.

Background/context:
- We observed intermittent tail spikes on customer workloads (mixed sequence lengths, many short prompts with occasional long continuations). Existing perf traces showed high kernel runtime variance even when p99 input size was stable.
- Hypothesis: certain kernel granularities cause L2 thrash / bank conflicts for real sequence mixes, especially when fused ops combine attention + feed-forward for small micro-batches.

Setup and methodology:
- Hardware: NVIDIA A100 40GB (PCIe) on staging cluster pool-a2 (pools/infra-qa-3).
- Runtime build: serving-runtime@commit 9f3d2b (profiling flags enabled), FlashAttention branch: fa-quant-patch (PR 812).
- Perf tools: nvprof deprecated, used Nsight Systems + custom nvtx spans, cupti counter aggregation, and per-kernel sample collection via perfetto.
- Workloads: three synthetic mixes to simulate production:
  1) Short-heavy: 90% seq=32 token prompts, 10% seq=1024 continuations (microbatch B=8 steady).
  2) Varied: uniform mix across {16,32,64,128,512,1024} with Poisson arrival.
  3) Burst/long: frequent short bursts then a long sequence tail; tests with prefix cache hits enabled/disabled.
- Sweep parameters: tile sizes {32,64,128}, warp-coarsening factors {1,2,4}, fused-op bundling on/off (i.e., attempt to collapse attention+addnorm+ffn into single kernel), KV caching on/off.
- Measurement focus: kernel latency distribution (p50/p90/p99), L2 read/write throughput, L1/shared hit ratios, warp occupancy, SM utilization, memory stalls (as % cycles). Also derived heatmaps mapping sequence length vs tile-size showing p99 latency and L2 bandwidth density.

Quick reproducible command snippets (staging):
- Launch trace: ./run_bench --workload varied --batch 8 --duration 300 --nvtx && nsys profile --output out.qdrep --trace=nvtx ./run_bench ...
- Extract counters: python tools/trace_extract.py --qdrep out.qdrep --counters l2_throughput,l1_hit,sm_efficiency --out heatmap.csv
- Microbench per-kernel: python tools/kernel_runner.py --kernel flash --tile 64 --warp 2 --seq 512 --repeat 1000 --out kernel-run.json

Findings (summary):
1) Two distinct failure modes emerged:
   - Mode A (L2 thrash): For tile sizes >= 128 combined with high warp-coarsening (4) on moderate seq (256-512), L2 read throughput spikes and p99 kernel latency doubles compared to tile 64. Heatmap shows concentrated L2 read density aligned with sequences 256-512.
   - Mode B (shared-bank/warp divergence): Fused-op bundles for short sequences (<=64) reduce overall instruction overhead but create bank conflict patterns in shared memory when >1 fused instance runs per SM. This manifests as increased memory stalls and p90 jitter.

2) FlashAttention vs Paged Attention
   - FlashAttention (optimized tiled kernel) performs best on uniform large sequences (>512) when tile 64/warp2; it suffers Mode A when tile is too large relative to the per-request seq distribution because the kernel's memory access stride pattern induces L2 evictions across concurrent requests.
   - Paged attention (flash-paged style) is more robust to mixed small/large mixes due to its page-based prefetching but shows consistently higher fixed overhead for short sequences, leading to worse median but better p99 in mixed workloads.

3) Fused ops interactions
   - Combining attention+postnorm+ffn into one fused kernel reduces token-level overhead by ~18% for B=8 when seq <= 64. However, for varied sequences, fused kernels amplify Mode B due to shared-memory reuse patterns across the compound op.

Representative data (selected results):
- Varied mix (B=8):
  - FlashAttention tile=64 warp=2: p50=11.2ms p90=28.6ms p99=68.3ms L2_read=380GB/s
  - FlashAttention tile=128 warp=4: p50=13.1ms p90=33.9ms p99=142.7ms L2_read=680GB/s (spike)
  - Paged attention page=32KB: p50=14.9ms p90=31.2ms p99=82.4ms L2_read=420GB/s
- Short-heavy (B=8, fused on):
  - Fused tile=64: median improves by 16% but p90 increases by 22% when concurrency > 12 streams due to shared bank stalls.

Visual artifacts (description of heatmaps and traces):
- Heatmap: x-axis = sequence length bucket, y-axis = tile size. Color = p99 latency. Distinct hot vertical band at seq 256-512 for tile 128.
- Counter overlay: L2 read throughput heat overlay correlates with p99 hot zones.
- Flame graphs: fused-op flame shows long shared-memory wait slices for SM3/SM5 when multiple fused kernels are scheduled concurrently.

Root cause hypotheses validated:
- Large tile sizes combined with high warp-coarsening increase working set footprint of a single kernel in L2; when several such kernels run concurrently (multi-stream), the cumulative footprint exceeds L2 capacity resulting in eviction storms and increased DRAM fetches.
- Fused ops increase intra-kernel shared-memory pressure; when multiple fused kernels allocate shared segments, bank conflicts and serialization occur, hurting p90/p99.

Mitigations and proposed heuristics:
1) Runtime kernel selector: prefer tile size 64 for mixed workloads and avoid increasing warp-coarsening beyond 2 unless the observed seq distribution median > 512 AND measured L2 pressure < threshold. Implement quick check: sample 200 requests over 30s to estimate median seq and current L2 occupancy.
2) Fused-op admission control: enable fused kernels only when concurrency < N_fused (experimentally ~10 streams for A10040) OR when average seq <= 64. Otherwise fall back to un-fused pipeline.
3) Backpressure & adaptive batching: if L2 read throughput crosses 550GB/s for >5s, throttle new large-tile kernels by shifting new requests to paged attention or smaller tile variants.
4) Telemetry: add a lightweight heatmap sampler to the agent that emits tile x seq buckets with p50/p90/p99 and L2 counters every minute; surface in Console as "kernel locality heatmap".

Confidence and caveats:
- Confidence: medium-high for A100-like GPUs; less certainty for H100 because its L2 architecture and caching are different. Re-run suite on H100.
- Caveat: experiments used synthetic mixes; production traces show more subtle temporal correlations (bursts) that can exacerbate thrash. Need to test with recorded production replay (ask infra for replay token).

Action items (practical next steps):
- [ ] Add sampler telemetry proto: small payload documenting tile/warp/seq bucket counters (Samir). JIRA-INF-2345 assigned.
- [ ] Implement runtime kernel selector with safe default (tile=64, warp<=2) and feature-flagged aggressive mode (Asha). Target PR: draft against runtime/auto-kernel-select branch.
- [ ] Run full sweep on H100 testbed (Diego) and compare L2 thresholds; capture heatmaps.
- [ ] Add unit e2e replay harness that replays a 2-hour production trace into the staging pool with nvtx tagging (Lena).
- [ ] Postmortem draft if customer incident reproducible: summarize root cause and timeline (owner TBD).

Open questions for team discussion:
- Should we expose tile/warp knobs to customers (opt-in) or keep as internal runtime choice? (Pros: transparency for power users; Cons: complexity and risk of misconfiguration)
- What is the acceptable tradeoff between median improvement and p99 risk for PLG default?

Notes to self / quick pointers:
- Useful Slack thread: #runtime-perf (see thread ts=1697xxxxxx).
- Perf script: tools/heatmap_v2.py is handy for converting qdrep -> png; it assumes csv columns (seq,tile,p99,l2_read).
- Replay corpus location: gs://redwood-prod-replays/2025-10/ (request access via infra).

Appendix: raw experiment command examples and snippets
- kernel-runner script call for heatmap sweep:
  python tools/kernel_runner.py --mode sweep --tiles "32,64,128" --warps "1,2,4" --seqs "16,32,64,128,256,512,1024" --repeat 200 --out sweep-results.csv

- quick NVTX annotation pattern used:
  nvtx::range_push("kernel:fa:tile64:warp2:seq512"); run_kernel(...); nvtx::range_pop();

- example quick-check telemetry payload (proto text):
  tile_bucket: 64
  seq_bucket: 256
  samples: 187
  p50_ms: 12.4
  p90_ms: 29.1
  p99_ms: 71.9
  l2_read_gb_s: 432.1

If helpful I can convert this labnote into a short PR checklist and a draft runtime change (proto + selector) to review next week. For now, saving these notes and starting the PR branch for the selector.

-- Asha
